Random effects model

Source: R/random_effects.R
random_effects.Rd

Models the joint distribution of the test results with one continuous latent variable \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\), independent of the disease and that can be read as the severity of the condition. Within each disease class the tests are independent given \(Z\), and they are dependent overall because they share \(Z\). The model needs at least two tests.

Usage

random_effects(
  prevalence_prior = prior_beta(0.5, 2),
  intercepts_prior = prior_normal(0, 1.5),
  loadings_prior = prior_normal(0, 1),
  positive_loadings = TRUE,
  verification = mar()
)

Arguments

prevalence_prior

Prior on the prevalence \(\pi\): a single prior, either on a probability, such as prior_beta(), which acts on \(\pi\), or on the real line, such as prior_normal(), which acts on \(\mathrm{logit}\,\pi\). Default prior_beta(0.5, 2), the uniform distribution on (0, 1).

intercepts_prior

Prior on the marginal probits \(m_{dk}\), a real-valued prior applied to all \(2K\) values (\(K\) tests for each class) with the same prior, for example prior_normal(). For the diseased class it is a prior on the probit of the sensitivity, for the healthy class on the probit of one minus the specificity. Default prior_normal(0, 1.5).

loadings_prior

Prior on the loadings \(b_{dk}\), a real-valued prior applied to all \(2K\) loadings with the same prior, for example prior_normal(). If positive_loadings = TRUE the prior is restricted to positive values for all loadings; if FALSE it is restricted to positive values only for the first loading of each class, the others are real. Default prior_normal(0, 1).

positive_loadings

A single logical value, TRUE or FALSE, not NA. If TRUE (default), all the loadings are positive, so the tests can only be positively dependent within each class. If FALSE, only the first loading of each class is positive and the others can take any sign, which can make the sampler unreliable. See Details for why a constraint is needed and how the two options behave.

verification

Verification mechanism: an object of class mar (default, mar()) or mnar(). The priors of the verification mechanism (for example verification = mnar(odds_ratio_prior = prior_normal(0, 1), by_profile = TRUE)) are set in that object, not in this function.

Value

An object of class random_effects.

Details

Let \(t = (t_1, \dots, t_K)\) be a response profile, with \(t_k = 1\) for a positive result, and \(d \in \{0, 1\}\) the disease status. Given \(D = d\) and \(Z = z\), the test results are independent and $$P(T_k = 1 \mid D = d, Z = z) = \Phi(a_{dk} + b_{dk} z),$$ where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function, \(a_{dk}\) is an intercept and \(b_{dk}\) a loading, for each test \(k\) and class \(d\). The model has \(2K\) intercepts and loadings per class, plus the prevalence \(\pi = P(D = 1)\). This is the Gaussian random effects (probit latent variable) model for conditional dependence between tests (Qu et al., 1996; Dendukuri and Joseph, 2001).

Integrating out \(Z\) gives the probability of each profile in class \(d\), \(\theta_{d,t} = P(T = t \mid D = d)\): $$\theta_{d,t} = \int \prod_{k=1}^{K} \Phi(a_{dk} + b_{dk} z)^{t_k}\, [1 - \Phi(a_{dk} + b_{dk} z)]^{1 - t_k}\,\phi(z)\,dz,$$ where \(\phi\) is the standard normal density. The integral is computed with 32-node Gauss-Hermite quadrature.

Integrating out \(Z\) also gives the marginal probits $$P(T_k = 1 \mid D = d) = \Phi(m_{dk}), \qquad m_{dk} = \frac{a_{dk}}{\sqrt{1 + b_{dk}^2}},$$ so that the sensitivity of test \(k\) is \(Se_k = \Phi(m_{1k})\) and its specificity is \(Sp_k = 1 - \Phi(m_{0k})\). The model is sampled in the marginal probits \(m_{dk}\), which the data inform directly, and \(a_{dk} = m_{dk}\sqrt{1 + b_{dk}^2}\).

The loadings describe the dependence between the tests within each class. Given \(D = d\), the covariance between tests \(j\) and \(k\) has the sign of \(b_{dj} b_{dk}\): a positive product means the tests tend to agree beyond what the disease explains, a negative product means they tend to disagree. The size of the loadings sets the strength of the dependence, and a loading close to 0 makes its test almost independent of the others in that class. Loadings are specific to each class, so the dependence can differ between diseased and healthy subjects.

Let \(n_{t,1}\) and \(n_{t,0}\) be the numbers of verified diseased and verified healthy subjects with profile \(t\), \(u_t\) the number of unverified subjects with profile \(t\), \(\pi_1 = \pi\) and \(\pi_0 = 1 - \pi\). The log-likelihood of the aggregated data is $$\ell = \sum_t \Big[\sum_{d} n_{t,d} \log(\pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}\, \lambda_{t,d}) + u_t \log \sum_{d} \pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}\,(1 - \lambda_{t,d})\Big],$$ where \(\lambda_{t,d} = P(V = 1 \mid T = t, D = d)\) is the probability of verification. Dependence models with partial verification of this kind are discussed by Albert and Dodd (2008).

With verification = mar() (missing at random) the verification probability does not depend on the disease status (Rubin, 1976), so the verification terms carry no information on the parameters and are dropped: $$\ell = \sum_t \Big[\sum_{d} n_{t,d} \log(\pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}) + u_t \log \sum_{d} \pi_d\,\theta_{d,t}\Big] + \textrm{const.}$$

With verification = mnar() (missing not at random) the verification probability depends on the disease status (Kosinski and Barnhart, 2003): \(\mathrm{logit}\,\lambda_{t,d} = \alpha_t + \beta d\) for every profile with at least one verified subject, while \(\lambda_{t,d} = 0\) for profiles that are never verified. The parameter \(\beta\) is the log odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same profile; \(\beta > 0\) means that the diseased are verified more often, and \(\exp(-\beta)\) is the odds ratio of disease between unverified and verified subjects with the same profile. With by_profile = TRUE in verification = mnar(by_profile = TRUE), each profile has its own \(\beta_t\).

The data do not inform every parameter directly. The probabilities \(\theta_{d,t}\) of the profiles that are never verified are determined only by the assumed latent structure, and under MNAR the parameter \(\beta\) is also informed only by that structure. Both depend on the correctness of the model, so the results on these quantities are fragile if the structure is wrong (Albert and Dodd, 2004).

Constraint on the signs of the loadings. Since \(Z\) and \(-Z\) have the same distribution, changing the sign of all the loadings of a class gives exactly the same profile probabilities: the parameters \((a_{d1}, \dots, a_{dK}, b_{d1}, \dots, b_{dK})\) and \((a_{d1}, \dots, a_{dK}, -b_{d1}, \dots, -b_{dK})\) fit the data equally well. Without a constraint the posterior would have two mirror-image modes, and different chains could settle in different ones. Two constraints are available:

  • positive_loadings = TRUE (default): all the loadings are positive. The mirror image is excluded entirely, and every pair of tests is positively dependent within each class: the tests tend to err together, as is usual for tests that measure the same condition. Negative dependence cannot be represented.

  • positive_loadings = FALSE: only the first loading of each class is positive, the others can take any sign, so any sign of dependence is allowed. This removes the mirror image only when the first loading is clearly away from 0. When it is close to 0, for example because the first test is nearly independent of the others, the mirror-image configuration (first loading near 0, the others with the opposite sign) can be reached continuously, and the posterior keeps a second mode. Chains that settle in different modes give different estimates (R-hat well above 1), and the sampler can produce divergent transitions near the boundary. On simulated data with dependent tests this happens in most fits. Use this option only when negative dependence is plausible, with several chains, and check that the chains agree.

References

Albert, P. S. and Dodd, L. E. (2004). A cautionary note on the robustness of latent class models for estimating diagnostic error without a gold standard. Biometrics, 60(2), 427–435. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2004.00187.x

Albert, P. S. and Dodd, L. E. (2008). On estimating diagnostic accuracy from studies with multiple raters and partial gold standard evaluation. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 103(481), 61–73. doi:10.1198/016214507000000329

Dendukuri, N. and Joseph, L. (2001). Bayesian approaches to modeling the conditional dependence between multiple diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 57(1), 158–167. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00158.x

Kosinski, A. S. and Barnhart, H. X. (2003). Accounting for nonignorable verification bias in assessment of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 59(1), 163–171. doi:10.1111/1541-0420.00019

Qu, Y., Tan, M. and Kutner, M. H. (1996). Random effects models in latent class analysis for evaluating accuracy of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 52(3), 797–810. doi:10.2307/2533043

Rubin, D. B. (1976). Inference and missing data. Biometrika, 63(3), 581–592. doi:10.1093/biomet/63.3.581

Examples

random_effects()
#> <random_effects> random effects model, Gauss-Hermite quadrature
#>   prevalence_prior: Beta(mean = 0.5, precision = 2)
#>   intercepts_prior: Normal(mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
#>   loadings_prior:   Normal(mean = 0, sd = 1), all loadings positive
#>   verification:     mar
random_effects(positive_loadings = FALSE)
#> <random_effects> random effects model, Gauss-Hermite quadrature
#>   prevalence_prior: Beta(mean = 0.5, precision = 2)
#>   intercepts_prior: Normal(mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
#>   loadings_prior:   Normal(mean = 0, sd = 1), first loading positive
#>   verification:     mar
